questions.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}5x-1y \\ -10x+2y\end{aligned}]$
and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 8\end{aligned}].$
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each vector ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}24 \\ -48\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}10 \\ 8\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}42 \\ -84\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{2})=0,$ we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,T$ is $\,{v}_{2}.$

choices.value: None of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $T$

questions.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-y+z \\ -6x+3y-3z \\ 4x-2y+2z\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ k\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}2\cdot 3-1+k \\ -6\cdot 3+3\cdot 1-3\cdot k \\ 4\cdot 3-2\cdot 1+2\cdot k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5+k \\ -15-3k \\ 10+2k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}5+k=0 \\ -15-3k=0 \\ 10+2k=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to all three of these equations is $k=-5.$

questions.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z \\ -12x-4y+4z \\ 6x+8y+10z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=-2z.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z & =0 \\ -9x-3(-2z)+3z & =0 \\ -9x+9z & =0 \\ x & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is ${[\begin{aligned}z \\ -2z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R}.$

questions.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-4y+2z \\ x-3y+z \\ 4x-4y+z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x,$ $y,$ and $z.$ From the third equation, we obtain $z=0$ and from the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is ${[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}.$

questions.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-6x+y \\ 12x-2y\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 12 & -2\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 12 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=\frac{1}{6}y.
$$

 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{aligned}]y,\,y\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

questions.problem:
Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x-8y \\ 16y-6x\end{aligned}],$
find  $2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $2$nd one). 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3=2\cdot 1-3=-1.
$$

\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 8 & -3 & 10 \\ -6 & 3 & -9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ -6 & 3 & -9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot columns (the third one). Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.
$$

First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -6 \\ 0 & -8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=0.$

$$

$$

Consider the linear transformation

and the vectors 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/4fbbb82838d7fa94fe0aeb47ed48952bfe573e12874d3891f8650a15b46e0ee7.png)
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $\mathbf{T}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A vector $\mathbf{u}$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ if $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_i)$ for each vector $\mathbf v_i\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)=\mathbf{0},$ we conclude that, of the given vectors, the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,\mathbf{T}$ is $\,\mathbf{v}_1.$
